Technical Guide

How DoubleFloats represents numbers and which algorithms sit behind the public functions. For guidance on extending the package, see Adding New Functions.

Representation: unevaluated sums

A DoubleFloat{T} holds two floats, hi and lo, whose unevaluated sum is the represented value:

value = hi + lo,   with   |lo| ≤ ulp(hi)/2

hi is the value rounded to T; lo is the leading part of the rounding error. For Double64 this yields a 106-bit significand (2 × 53), about 32 decimal digits, with one ulp ≈ 2⁻¹⁰⁴ relative.

Two structural consequences matter throughout the package:

  • The exponent range is that of T. Overflow and underflow happen where Float64 overflows and underflows.
  • Precision degrades near the bottom of the range. When |value| < ~4e-292, the lo word is subnormal and the effective precision tapers below 106 bits; below ~1e-308 only Float64 precision remains. This is a representation limit — visible, for example, in exp(x) for x < -670 — and no algorithm returning a Double64 can beat it.

Error-free transformations

All arithmetic reduces to a handful of exact building blocks (src/math/errorfree.jl):

  • two_sum(a, b) / two_hilo_sum(a, b): hi + lo == a + b exactly.
  • two_prod(a, b): hi + lo == a * b exactly, using fma.
  • Division and square root use these plus one Newton-like correction (src/math/ops/), giving faithfully rounded (≤ 1 ulp) results.

A subtlety worth knowing: a zero lo word does not mean a value is exact, and no fast path may skip the correction step because of it (inv once did, and silently returned Float64-quality reciprocals for inputs like Double64(3.0)).

Elementary function algorithms

Exponential functions (src/math/elementary/explog.jl). The shared base-2 kernel reduces the exponent to n + 8r with |r| ≲ 1/16. It evaluates a tapered polynomial for 2^r using fused Horner steps, squares three times, and reconstructs with a split power-of-two scale. exp and exp10 use three-limb base conversion on the native path.

Inputs safely below the zero-rounding threshold bypass the polynomial. In the underflow band, both reduced limbs contribute to rounding on the target format's subnormal grid. If the error bound overlaps a rounding midpoint, the fallback evaluates the original input with directed MPFR rounding and increases precision until the bounds agree. An exact input sum lets one downward evaluation and its next representable MPFR value bound an inexact result. The fallback compiles on first use. Ordinary Double32 calls to exp promote through Double64, with direct rounding to the Float32 grid in the underflow band.

Logarithms. The log2 kernel decomposes a positive input into an exponent and a mantissa. It uses 32 exact table centers c and a polynomial in t², where t = (m-c)/(m+c) for mantissa m. Near one it uses t = (x-1)/(x+1) directly to preserve the small result. The table path rescales tiny inputs and checks both source and destination exponent fields before adjusting the low limb's exponent. This matters even when the low limb starts out normal. log and log10 convert the log2 result to their respective bases.

log1p and expm1. Near zero, log1p uses log(1+x) = 2·atanh(x/(2+x)). expm1 evaluates a Taylor series on a scaled argument and reconstructs with the doubling identity expm1(2t) = expm1(t)·(expm1(t) + 2).

Cube root and fused multiply-add. Scalar cbrt returns a DoubleFloat. For extreme Double64 inputs it scales both limbs by 2^(-3k) before Newton refinement and scales the root by 2^k afterward. This keeps intermediate products in range and retains the input's low-limb contribution at working precision. Near cancellation, fma and muladd for three Double64 operands refine the result with an allocation-free expansion. Its tuple capacity grows one slot at a time as product and addend terms are inserted.

Trigonometric functions (trig.jl): argument reduction by mod2pi, then circle-splitting into [0, π/32] segments with tabulated sin/cos anchor values and short Taylor kernels. Reductions near the roots (x - π/2, x - π) carry a triple-double π so cancellation does not eat the low word. Branch windows must be bounded: each Taylor kernel is only valid for |r| ≤ π/32.

Hyperbolics: from exp(±x); sinh/cosh switch to a Float128 route above 709 where exp alone would overflow although they remain finite (through ln(2·floatmax) ≈ 710.476).

Inverse hyperbolics (archyptrig.jl): formulated to keep relative precision at their sensitive points, and to avoid squaring overflow:

functionsmall/near-1 formlarge-argument form (≥ 4/eps)
asinhlog1p(x + x²/(1+√(1+x²)))log(x) + ln2
acoshlog1p(u + √(u(2+u))), u = x-1 exactlog(x) + ln2
atanh½·log1p(2x/(1-x))½·(log1p(x) - log1p(-x)) for x > ½

acsch, asech, acoth delegate with exactly-formed intermediates (e.g. acoth = ½·log1p(2/(x-1))), never through a bare inv(x) where that would lose 1/x - 1.

agm / ellipk (src/math/special/): the AGM iteration stops when the gap |a-b| stops shrinking — its quadratic convergence ends exactly at the roundoff floor — rather than testing a fixed tolerance, which cannot be chosen correctly in advance for all operand scales.

erf, erfc, gamma, Bessel: computed via Float128 (Quadmath), whose 113-bit significand slightly exceeds Double64 working precision.

Elementary vector kernels

The User Guide describes DoubleFloats.simdmap!, including axes, overlapping inputs, and exceptions. The driver checks storage and element types once per call. The batch kernels reuse the scalar coefficients and error-free transforms without reassociation or @fastmath. They operate on the ordinary interleaved arrays of high and low limbs.

For a native route, the driver checks both limbs in blocks of up to 32 or 64 elements, depending on the operation. The intervals below bound the high word. The low word must be finite and at most half the high word's binade ulp in magnitude. The bounds leave room for the low limb and nested intermediate operations. Vectors shorter than 64 elements take the scalar path.

Input type and operationsNative ranges and result
Double64 exp2Heads on −1021 to −0.001 or 0.001 to 1023, where the high word of the result stays normal.
Double64 exp, exp10Absolute head from 0.001 to 700 for exp and from 0.001 to 300 for `exp10), with three-limb base conversion.
Double64 log2, log, log10Direct regime strictly between 15/16 and 17/16. Table regime at or above 2^-915 outside the direct interval, up to the largest finite head.
Double64 log1p, expm1log1p on 0.005–0.05. expm1 uses four doublings for absolute heads on [2^-5, 2^-4) and ordinary exponential subtraction on 0.5–700.
Double64 powerScalar Int exponent 5 with bases on 0.5–1.5, or vector Double64 exponents on 0.2–0.9 with bases on 1.1–1.5.
Double64 sin, cos, sincosAbsolute head from 0.005 up to 6.28125 radians, exclusive of the upper bound. sincos writes a tuple.
Double64 tanSame head interval, with a 0.11-radian exclusion around the heads of π/2 and 3π/2 in the absolute angle.
Double64 cisAbsolute heads on 0.005–0.09 and strictly between the direct Taylor cutoff (approximately 0.09817) and 6.28125. Writes a complex result.
Double64 hypot, DoubleFloats.normalizeBoth absolute heads on 0.25–8. normalize writes a tuple in input order.
Double64 invAbsolute head from 2^-256 through 2^256.
Double64 cot, unary atanPositive heads on 0.005–0.09 and 0.005–0.19, respectively.
Double64 hyperbolic functionssinh, cosh, tanh, csch, sech, and coth on 1.1–5.
Double64 inverse hyperbolic functionsasinh on 0.005–0.045, acosh on 1.00002–1.001, atanh on 0.005–0.025, acsch on 30–50, asech on 0.999–0.99998, and acoth on 40–100.
ComplexDF64 square, abs2, exp, sinh, coshReal head on 1.1–5 and imaginary head on 0.005–0.09. abs2 writes a real result.
ComplexDF64 sin, cos, tan, cot, DoubleFloats.csc, DoubleFloats.secImaginary head on 1.1–5. Real head on 0.005–0.09 for sin and cos, or 0.005–0.045 for the other four.
ComplexDF64 tanh, coth, csch, sechReal head on 1.1–5 and imaginary head on 0.005–0.045.

Mixed blocks normally use the scalar loop, which preserves exception order. The circular kernels prefer the small-angle route and then try the wider circular reduction. The wider route reuses the three-limb π reductions and resolves the table sector using both input limbs. For exp2, sin, cos, tan, and wider cis, a block with at most one eighth of its lanes excluded can SIMD-evaluate safe substitute inputs and then repair those lanes with the original scalar calls. This requires every excluded input to pass a wider check that makes the scalar calls and assignments safe. Blocks containing a potential domain error go through the scalar loop before any element of the block is written.

The pi-scaled trig functions, binary atan and DoubleFloats.atanxy, and the inverse circular functions other than unary Double64 atan use the existing scalar algorithms inside the batch. The same applies to complex sqrt, log, and the inverse complex functions. This preserves special values, signed zeros, argument quadrants, and complex branch cuts. Threaded calls use contiguous chunks. Most supported operations are eligible from 4,096 elements. For Double64, hypot and paired normalize are eligible from 16,384 elements. Reciprocal and integer power use a 65,536-element threshold.

Batch benchmarks

The table reports median microseconds per 4,096 elements from 11 interleaved measurements. It uses the bounded fixtures in perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl, seed 0x5eed, Julia 1.13.3, and native AVX2/FMA targeting on an Intel Core i9-14900K. The baseline is preallocated scalar broadcast from revision d68a1c0c. The batch column includes dispatch and lane checks.

OperationBaseline broadcast (µs)Serial batch (µs)Speedup
sin135.034.53.9×
sincos149.741.43.6×
Unary atan375.479.54.7×
exp2112.934.73.3×
Fixed-binade expm1360.093.93.8×
Table log110.933.13.3×
Power with scalar exponent 541.95.97.1×
ComplexDF64 exp430.671.26.0×

These batch runs used zero heap allocations after compilation. LLVM's native-target output showed loop vectorization across elements in the admitted kernels. Julia 1.10.10 with the Haswell target used scalar loops for some of the same compositions, including tuple-output sincos and vector-exponent power. Performance depends on the compiler and target. With 1% shuffled out-of-window inputs, sparse repair gave 2.2–2.7× over scalar broadcast for sin, cos, tan, and exp2. The same fixtures gave 1.4–1.6× when entire mixed blocks used the scalar loop. Clustered exclusions leave more eligible blocks intact. Fully excluded fixtures ran near scalar speed. In the separate Julia 1.10.10 exponential tests, zero-only exp2 was about 0.9× and MPFR midpoint repair took about 9.7 ms for 4,096 elements in both the scalar and serial batch runs. On a general-range run with 65,536 elements per case, the median across the original 71 cases was 1.0× for serial batching and 2.0× with four workers relative to scalar broadcast. A caller-managed threaded scalar loop also gave 2.0× on that run.

The expanded paths were measured against the public serial batch API at revision 9b4a13cf on the same CPU and Julia 1.13.3. These are medians from 13 interleaved timings of 65,536 elements with one Julia thread and no warmed heap allocations.

Operations and input headsSpeedup over the previous batch API

hypot and paired normalize on independent positive pairs from 0.25–84.2× and 2.0×
inv on −128–1282.1×

The compiler emitted vector loops for the converted exponentials, positive-pair hypot, reciprocal, and the masked wide tan kernel on this target. The wider circular pair and paired normalization also benefited from the checked arithmetic when LLVM emitted scalar loops. The sin, cos, and sincos fixtures on −100–100 ran near their previous throughput because few lanes fell within one circle.

Run the driver from the package root. Its output includes the measured range, storage, seed, Julia and CPU versions, CPU target, thread count, revision, median and spread, allocations, and first-use time. For a pre-change comparison, run the same driver with --baseline and the older checkout as the active project.

julia --project -t4 perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl
SIMD_RANGE=general SIMD_SIZE=65536 julia --project -t4 perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl
SIMD_MIXTURE=0,0.01,0.1,0.5,1 SIMD_FILTER='^(sin|exp2|log)$' \
    julia --project perf/bench_simd_elementary.jl

Set SIMD_CLUSTERED=1 for clustered mixtures, SIMD_LOG_REGIMES=1 for repeated table indices and direct/table mixtures, or SIMD_RANGE=special for poles, exponential underflow, and MPFR midpoint repair. The driver also supports comma-separated sizes, SIMD_STORAGE=strided, narrow, or alias, alternative whole-block widths via SIMD_BLOCK_SIZES, and native IR dumps into the directory given by SIMD_LLVM. For dense calls, the driver prints lane eligibility counts for the installed regimes. Eligible lanes can still use scalar code when a whole block fails its checks.

The repository's docs/vecbetter.md records the phased rollout and the numerical results for binary atan.

Linear algebra

LAPACK covers only Float32/64 and their complexes, so DoubleFloats routes dense factorizations through pure-Julia generic implementations:

  • lu, qr, \: LinearAlgebra's generic kernels.
  • eigen, eigvals, schur, hessenberg: GenericSchur (QR iteration). DoubleFloats owns explicit eigen/eigvals methods (src/math/linearalgebra/eigen.jl) that pin this routing, detect hermitian input (tridiagonalization + symmetric QR: real eigenvalues, orthonormal vectors), and normalize output conventions to match the LAPACK route (real Eigen for a real spectrum, (real, imag) sorting, unit-norm vectors).
  • svd: GenericLinearAlgebra.
  • sylvester/lyap (sylvester.jl): Bartels–Stewart — Schur factorizations of both operands, triangular back-substitution, transform back.
  • lq: the generic Householder QR of the adjoint, repackaged as an LQ factorization (A = L·Q ⟺ A′ = Q_qr·R), with the missing LQPackedQ materialization/multiplication kernels supplied for DoubleFloat element types.

Matrix functions

src/math/linearalgebra/matfun.jl; all correct for defective matrices:

  • exp: scaling-and-squaring; scale to ‖A‖₁ ≤ 1, a 34-term Taylor approximant (truncation < 1/35! ≈ 1e-40) evaluated by Paterson–Stockmeyer (≈ 11 matrix products), then repeated squaring. Real input never leaves real arithmetic.
  • sqrt: complex Schur + the Björck–Hammarling recurrence on the triangular factor; hermitian-PSD input shortcuts through eigen.
  • log: complex Schur + inverse scaling-and-squaring — repeated triangular square roots until ‖T - I‖₁ ≤ ¼, then the atanh series (re-using inv_oddint), then multiply by 2^s.
  • trig/hyperbolic: one shared-power series pair in Y = B² plus double-angle recurrences (cos(2X) = 2cos²X - I, sin(2X) = 2 sin X cos X — and the same formulas for cosh/sinh), entirely in the input's arithmetic, so real matrices never touch complex intermediates.
  • hermitian input (exact ishermitian) short-circuits exp, trig, and hyperbolic functions through one symmetric eigen-decomposition — the orthonormal eigenvectors make that transform perfectly conditioned.
  • triangular input skips the Schur factorization entirely for sqrt/log (the recurrences apply directly; tril maps to triu through the transpose identity).
  • Real results that acquire ~1e-32 imaginary roundoff dust from a complex intermediate are stripped back to real (with a tolerance guard), matching LAPACK-route behavior.

cbrt, sinpi/cospi, and matrix inverse-trig/hyperbolic functions still use eigen-diagonalization (matrixfunction), which requires a diagonalizable argument and loses accuracy in proportion to cond(V).
